title: GiveDirectly pays over 4,600 people in Kogi State, Nigeria, on Google Flood Hub forecasts, mostly before floods peaked in October 2024
summary: GiveDirectly used Google Flood Hub forecasts to trigger $105 payments to over 4,600 people in Ibaji, Kogi State, most of them before floods peaked on 21 October 2024.
account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts through an application programming interface, made inundation maps and set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored the forecasts daily and cross-checked them with community observations. The trigger was met when forecasts showed that 20% of a community's area would flood, and verified residents were then paid. The New Humanitarian later described an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports that it sent $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. It paid 3,250 people between 29 August and 6 October 2024 and 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. In its own survey, GiveDirectly reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. On 14 October 2025 Rest of World reported that GiveDirectly planned a 2026 randomized trial of the approach in northern Bangladesh, covering over 100,000 families. The outlet gave 4,463 as the number of people paid early in Kogi, a lower figure than GiveDirectly's count of over 4,600. A note on GiveDirectly's page says that the page was updated in July 2026. On 31 August 2026 an investigation by The New Humanitarian found that data mismatches and barriers to phone access excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. GiveDirectly told the outlet that it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably.
purpose: Trigger and target anticipatory cash transfers to flood-prone communities before river flooding.
system: Google Flood Hub AI river-flood forecasts accessed via API, with JBA Global Resilience hydrology analysis and a 20%-of-community-area trigger rule
developer: Google (Flood Hub); trigger design by GiveDirectly with JBA Global Resilience
domain: Humanitarian anticipatory action and cash transfers
taxonomy_note: Cash paid before a forecast flood is read as reducing potential for harm; Trustible's description stresses legal harm.

ratings.reason: GiveDirectly sent $105 to over 4,600 individuals, and a $210 transfer followed. The sources do not state how many people received the second transfer. In its own survey, GiveDirectly reports that weekly income more than doubled and that food shortages fell. No independent source verifies these survey figures.

GiveDirectly gained a tested trigger pipeline and documented lessons. It acknowledged to The New Humanitarian that it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says that the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation was published on 31 August 2026.

The cash that reached about 4,600 people is the personal benefit already rated, and no source reports a measured change for the 53 communities as a whole. The New Humanitarian also documents that some of the poorest residents were excluded.

ai_role.statement: Decisive for timing and geography: GiveDirectly told The New Humanitarian that satellite/AI flood modeling determined which communities were paid and when. Individual eligibility was decided by non-AI verification (ward residence, Smile ID checks, call-center calls). The investigation identifies that as the main source of exclusions. GiveDirectly's own page attributes the late payments to identity checks in two wards.

fields.account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts through an application programming interface, made inundation maps and set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored the forecasts daily and cross-checked them with community observations. The trigger was met when forecasts showed that 20% of a community's area would flood, and verified residents were then paid. The New Humanitarian later described an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports that it sent $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. It paid 3,250 people between 29 August and 6 October 2024 and 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. In its own survey, GiveDirectly reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. On 14 October 2025 Rest of World reported that GiveDirectly planned a 2026 randomized trial of the approach in northern Bangladesh, covering over 100,000 families. The outlet gave 4,463 as the number of people paid early in Kogi, a lower figure than GiveDirectly's count of over 4,600. A note on GiveDirectly's page says that the page was updated in July 2026. On 31 August 2026 an investigation by The New Humanitarian found that data mismatches and barriers to phone access excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. GiveDirectly told the outlet that it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably.

ratings.reason: GiveDirectly sent $105 to over 4,600 individuals, and a $210 transfer followed. The sources do not state how many people received the second transfer. In its own survey, GiveDirectly reports that weekly income more than doubled and that food shortages fell. No independent source verifies these survey figures.

GiveDirectly gained a tested trigger pipeline and documented lessons. It acknowledged to The New Humanitarian that it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says that the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation was published on 31 August 2026.

The cash that reached about 4,600 people is the personal benefit already rated, and no source reports a measured change for the 53 communities as a whole. The New Humanitarian also documents that some of the poorest residents were excluded.
